title: Budget levies, climate update and culture plan direction
subtitle: Road salt advocacy, Uptown BIA levy, Erbsville Road demolition, Lincoln Road purchase and a Weber Street grocery proposal
overview: Council set the 2025 tax levies. It adopted a general municipal levy of $107,321,892, approved the Uptown Waterloo BIA levy of $767,805, and approved special service levies for several homes associations. Both by-laws were passed later in the meeting. These decide what residents' property taxes will fund this year.

Council re-affirmed its corporate and community greenhouse gas reduction targets and recognized a 40% cut in corporate emissions from 2010. It also asked staff to work with the Office of the CAO on how the Culture Plan evolves, including who is included or excluded, and to return with an action-oriented strategy. Council approved the purchase of 250 Lincoln Road, extended the terms of two Enova independent directors by a year, and allowed demolition of a dwelling at 665 Erbsville Road.

Council also urged the province to create limited liability legislation and a stakeholder advisory committee on road salt pollution {{vote:m15}}. An informal public meeting on a proposed grocery store at 200 Weber Street North took place with no decision; staff will report back later. Council met in closed session before the public meeting, and the minutes report no public outcome from it.

decisions.detail: Council adopted the 2025 General Levy By-law based on a final municipal levy of $107,321,892 {{vote:m13}}.
Council approved a 2025 levy of $767,805 on properties in the Uptown Waterloo BIA to fund its operating and capital costs {{vote:m9}}.
Council approved the 2025 levies for the Beechwood South, Beechwood II and Beechwood West #1 homes associations, and the related by-law {{vote:m12}}.
Council authorized the Mayor and Clerk to sign the agreement of purchase and sale for 250 Lincoln Road, subject to the City Solicitor's satisfaction {{vote:m5}}.
Council re-affirmed corporate and community greenhouse gas reduction targets and recognized a 40% corporate emissions reduction from 2010 {{vote:m6}}.

Council approved the benchmarking report and directed staff to work with the CAO's office on the Culture Plan's evolution, including who is included or excluded, and return with an action-oriented strategy {{vote:m7}}.
Council approved a demolition permit for the dwelling, waiving the site plan requirement and setting a five-year deadline to complete the replacement development {{vote:m14}}.
Council urged the province to develop limited liability legislation, contractor training and standard best practices, and to fund an expert advisory committee on salt pollution {{vote:m15}}.

debate: On the climate update, one councillor noted that the last stretch of emissions cuts is the hardest. Staff said the path for facilities is known, centred on electrifying recreation centres, and that grants and execution are the main needs. Staff also named vehicle supply and provincial and federal advocacy as challenges.

On the Culture Plan, one councillor was uncomfortable narrowing the next phase to an arts-only strategy, citing a funding gap for cultural festivals and events and few voices from cultural groups. Staff said the change followed consultation and that other events are still supported. Council chose to ask for more information rather than wait for the arts grants report.

At the Weber Street North grocery proposal's informal public meeting, councillors asked about noise from rooftop equipment and rear deliveries, fencing, lighting, snow storage, stray shopping carts and the reduced parking. Staff said many details would be settled at site plan, and a noise study would be updated then. Residential use above the store would be very difficult because of flood risk.

Two delegates on road salt said provincial rules are missing and that contractor liability and insurance costs push over-salting. They said contractor training and limited liability could reduce salt use. Council members noted they had heard municipal concerns about liability for years.
